questions.stem: A student lists the components of a coastal cliff site: sandstone, sea spray, kelp, seagrass, wind and rock pools. Which pair are both components of the hydrosphere?
options: Sea spray and the water in the rock pools
Sandstone and the water in the rock pools
Kelp and the seagrass growing offshore
Wind and the sea spray blown onshore
questions.explanation: The hydrosphere is all of Earth's water, so sea spray and rock pool water belong to it. Kelp and seagrass are living things and belong to the biosphere, even though they live in water.

questions.stem: Glaciers, ice sheets and sea ice are all part of the hydrosphere. Which term is often used for this frozen part of it?
options: The cryosphere
The lithosphere
The troposphere
The asthenosphere
questions.explanation: Frozen water on Earth makes up the cryosphere, which is usually treated as part of the hydrosphere. The lithosphere and asthenosphere are layers of the geosphere, and the troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Dead leaves, fungi and earthworms are mixed through the top layer of a forest soil. How is the soil best classified in an Earth systems study?
options: As part of the biosphere only, because it contains living organisms
As part of the hydrosphere only, because it holds water in its pores
As a zone where the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere overlap
As part of the geosphere only, because it is made of weathered rock
questions.explanation: Soil contains mineral grains from the geosphere, organisms and organic matter from the biosphere, water in its pores and air in its spaces, so it is a meeting place of all four spheres. Classifying it in one sphere ignores the other components it contains.

questions.stem: Which of these is a component of the atmosphere rather than a process in it?
options: Convection
Precipitation
Water vapour
Condensation
questions.explanation: Components are the things that make up a sphere, such as gases, water vapour and dust. Condensation, convection and precipitation are processes that move or change those components.

questions.stem: In a field study of a creek in the Adelaide Hills, which of these is a hidden process that students would need instruments or indirect evidence to detect?
options: Ducks feeding on plants at the edge
Groundwater seeping into the creek bed
Leaves falling onto the creek surface in autumn
Water flowing over a small rock ledge
questions.explanation: Groundwater discharge happens below the surface and out of sight, so it is detected with measurements such as water temperature, conductivity or piezometer levels. Falling leaves, flowing water and feeding ducks can all be seen directly.

questions.stem: Which is a hidden component of a eucalypt woodland, rather than a visible one?
options: Lichen growing on exposed granite rocks
Hollows in the trunks of older trees
Mycorrhizal fungal threads in the soil
Bark shed in strips at the base of trees
questions.explanation: Fungal threads that link roots run through the soil and are too fine to see without digging and magnification. Shed bark, lichen and tree hollows can all be observed on a walk through the woodland.

questions.stem: On a cloudless summer day, a paddock of wheat loses large amounts of water to the air, though nothing can be seen leaving it. Which hidden process accounts for most of this, and how could it be shown?
options: Condensation, shown by placing a cold glass among the wheat plants
Sublimation, shown by weighing a soil sample before and after drying
Transpiration, shown by bagging a plant and collecting condensed water
Infiltration, shown by measuring the rise of water in a nearby bore
questions.explanation: Water vapour leaves the leaves through stomata by transpiration, and a clear bag over a plant collects it as droplets. Infiltration moves water down into the soil, not into the air, and sublimation is ice changing to vapour, which does not happen in a summer paddock.

questions.stem: Students want to detect slow creep of soil down a hillside, which is too slow to see. Which observation would give the best evidence of it?
options: Rocks on the slope that are covered in lichen
Fence posts and tree trunks that lean downslope
Grass that is greener at the base of the slope
Puddles that form at the top of the slope after rain
questions.explanation: Soil creep moves the upper soil faster than deeper soil, so posts and trunks gradually tilt downslope. Greener grass, puddles and lichen do not show that soil is moving.

questions.stem: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide, becomes weakly acidic and slowly dissolves limestone. Which spheres interact in this process?
options: The geosphere, biosphere and hydrosphere
The atmosphere, hydrosphere and geosphere
The biosphere, atmosphere and geosphere
The hydrosphere, biosphere and atmosphere
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide comes from the atmosphere, the rain is part of the hydrosphere and the limestone is part of the geosphere. No living things are needed for this chemical weathering, so the biosphere is not involved.

questions.stem: Lichens growing on bare rock release weak organic acids that break down the rock surface. Which interaction does this show?
options: The atmosphere depositing the geosphere
The biosphere weathering the geosphere
The geosphere supplying the atmosphere
The hydrosphere eroding the biosphere
questions.explanation: Lichens are living organisms, so their acids are an example of biological weathering of rock. This is one way new soil begins to form on bare rock.

questions.stem: A lightning strike starts a bushfire in the Mount Lofty Ranges. Smoke drifts over the city, and heavy rain a month later washes ash into a reservoir. Which sequence of spheres does this chain pass through?
options: Geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, then atmosphere
Biosphere, geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere
Atmosphere, geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere
Atmosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere
questions.explanation: Lightning is an atmospheric process, it burns vegetation in the biosphere, the smoke returns to the atmosphere and the ash ends up in the reservoir water. The geosphere is not a step in this chain, although ash also settles on the soil.

questions.stem: In a mangrove forest, roots trap fine sediment carried in by the tide, and the coastline slowly builds seaward. Which statement best describes the interactions?
options: The biosphere changes how the hydrosphere deposits geosphere material
The geosphere changes how the biosphere takes up hydrosphere material
The hydrosphere changes how the atmosphere deposits biosphere material
The atmosphere changes how the geosphere erodes hydrosphere material
questions.explanation: The tide (hydrosphere) carries sediment (geosphere), and the roots (biosphere) slow the water so the sediment settles. The living mangroves are the cause of the change in deposition, which builds the land outwards.

questions.stem: In an Earth systems web of interactions for a farm, what does each arrow normally represent?
options: A component that belongs to two of the four spheres at the same time
A measurement taken by students at a particular site on the farm
A boundary that separates one of the four spheres from the others
A process that moves matter or energy from one component to another
questions.explanation: In a web of interactions the boxes are components and the arrows are processes, such as evaporation, uptake or erosion, that link them. Labelling each arrow with its process makes the web a model that can be tested.

questions.stem: A student's web of interactions for a wetland has arrows for rainfall, evaporation, plant uptake and decomposition, but none linking the wetland to groundwater. Why is this a weakness?
options: Every web of interactions must include an equal number of arrows per sphere
Groundwater exchange is too slow to affect a wetland on any time-scale
A hidden exchange of water and nutrients with the aquifer is left out
Groundwater is part of the geosphere, so it should not appear in a web
questions.explanation: Many wetlands gain or lose water through their beds, so leaving out groundwater misses a hidden pathway that can control water level and salinity. Groundwater belongs to the hydrosphere and is a normal part of a wetland web.

questions.stem: In a dry year, a waterhole shrinks, the remaining water becomes saltier and warmer, and fish die. Which description best fits this?
options: A dynamic relationship in which a change in one component alters others
A static relationship in which the components stay in fixed proportions
A closed relationship in which no matter crosses the waterhole boundary
A one-way relationship in which only the biosphere affects the hydrosphere
questions.explanation: Less water concentrates salt and lets the water heat faster, which lowers dissolved oxygen and kills fish, so the components change together. Matter clearly crosses the boundary, since water evaporates.

questions.stem: Clearing native vegetation in a catchment raises the water table, which brings salt to the surface, which kills more vegetation. How is this best described?
options: A one-off change that does not alter other components
A positive feedback loop that reinforces the original change
A negative feedback loop that returns the system to balance
A cyclic pattern that repeats regularly with the seasons each year
questions.explanation: Loss of vegetation leads, through the rising saline water table, to further loss of vegetation, so the change amplifies itself. A negative feedback would reduce the change rather than strengthen it.

questions.stem: Which of these is a human-induced change to the hydrosphere?
options: Melting of snow on mountains during a warm spring
A drought caused by a shift in regional wind patterns
Flooding of a low floodplain after an unusually wet winter season
Building a weir that lowers the flow reaching a river mouth
questions.explanation: A weir is a human structure that holds back water, so the reduced flow downstream is human-induced. Snowmelt, drought from wind shifts and floods after heavy rain are natural changes.

questions.stem: A coastal dune system is eroding. Which observation would most strongly suggest a human-induced cause rather than a natural one?
options: Erosion increased after a series of large winter storms struck the coast
Erosion is greatest where the dunes face the strongest prevailing winds
Erosion follows a long period of lower than average sea-level pressure
Erosion is worst along informal walking tracks through the dune plants
questions.explanation: Trampling along tracks destroys the plants that bind the sand, so erosion concentrated on tracks points to people. Storms, prevailing winds and pressure patterns are natural causes.

questions.stem: Over several decades, a river mouth closed more often and a lagoon behind it became saltier. Upstream water extraction increased over the same period, and so did the frequency of droughts. What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: Droughts alone must have caused the change because they are natural
Neither factor can be linked to the change because both increased
Both natural and human factors probably contributed to the change
Upstream extraction alone must have caused the change at the mouth
questions.explanation: When two possible causes change at the same time, the data cannot separate them without further evidence, such as flow modelling. It is reasonable to conclude that both may have contributed, but not that one alone was the cause.

questions.stem: A large volcanic eruption injects sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere. Which effect on another sphere would be expected over the following year or two?
options: Strong warming of the lower atmosphere as sulfate droplets trap infrared
A rise in global sea level as the eruption adds water to the oceans
Rapid growth of land plants worldwide as sulfur fertilises the soil
Slight cooling of the lower atmosphere as sulfate droplets reflect sunlight
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide forms sulfate aerosol droplets that reflect sunlight, causing a small, temporary global cooling. The aerosols fall out within a few years, so the effect does not last.

questions.stem: Which change in the Earth system takes place over the longest time-scale?
options: Alternation between El Nino and La Nina conditions
Seasonal filling and drying of a coastal wetland
Advance and retreat of ice sheets in an ice age
Opening of a new ocean basin by seafloor spreading
questions.explanation: A new ocean opens over tens of millions of years. Ice ages cycle over tens of thousands to around a hundred thousand years, ENSO over a few years, and wetland filling over a year.

questions.stem: Students compare three records from one place: daily air temperature over a month, sea level over 100 years, and rock layers spanning 2 million years. What do these records show about Earth system change?
options: Change happens at different time-scales, and each record shows a different one
Change happens at a single time-scale, and the three records simply repeat it
Only the rock record shows real change, because the others are too short
Only the temperature record shows change, because the others are too slow
questions.explanation: Each record resolves a different time-scale, from days to centuries to millions of years. Choosing the right record depends on which change is being studied, so no one record can show every kind of change.

questions.stem: A seagrass meadow is mapped from aerial photos taken every 10 years. Its area falls between two photos and then partly recovers by the next. Why might these photos miss important information?
options: Seagrass area only ever changes over millions of years, so photos fail
A sudden loss and recovery between photos would not be recorded
Aerial photos cannot show seagrass, which grows beneath the water
A ten-year interval is too short to detect any change in seagrass
questions.explanation: The sampling interval sets the shortest change a record can detect, so a die-off and recovery within a decade could be invisible. Seagrass can be mapped from aerial photos in clear, shallow water, and it can change within months.

questions.stem: Fertiliser runoff from farms in one catchment causes an algal bloom in a single estuary. At which spatial scale is this change mainly felt?
options: Local to regional
Global, across the planet
Continental
Hemispheric
questions.explanation: A bloom in one estuary fed by one catchment affects that area and its surroundings, so it is a local to regional change. Global changes, such as rising carbon dioxide, affect the whole planet.

questions.stem: Which example best shows a local change contributing to a global change?
options: Building a groyne traps sand on one side of a beach and erodes the other
Draining a swamp lowers the water table under nearby paddocks and houses
Clearing a forest releases carbon dioxide that mixes through the atmosphere
Damming a creek lowers the water level in a wetland a few kilometres away
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from one cleared forest spreads through the whole atmosphere and adds to global warming. The other examples have effects that stay within a local area.

questions.stem: Dust storms in central Australia carry iron-rich dust far out over the Southern Ocean, where it can boost phytoplankton growth. What does this show?
options: Changes in the biosphere happen only where the change first began
Changes in one region can affect conditions in a distant region
Changes in one sphere never cross into another of the spheres
Changes in the atmosphere are always confined to a single place
questions.explanation: Wind carries dust from the geosphere in one region through the atmosphere to the hydrosphere and biosphere far away. Iron is a limiting nutrient for phytoplankton in parts of the Southern Ocean.

questions.stem: Which change in the Earth system is cyclic?
options: A landslide after a heavy storm
A meteorite striking the desert floor
An oil spill from a damaged ship
The daily rise and fall of the tide
questions.explanation: Tides rise and fall on a regular, predictable cycle driven by the Moon and Sun. Landslides, meteorite impacts and oil spills are one-off events that cannot be timed in advance.

questions.stem: Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre is usually a dry salt pan, but fills after rare, very heavy rain far to its north-east. How is this pattern best described?
options: Regular and predictable by the calendar date
Cyclic with a fixed period of about one year
Constant, with the lake level never changing
Irregular and hard to predict far in advance
questions.explanation: Filling depends on unusual rain events in a distant catchment, so it happens at irregular intervals that cannot be forecast years ahead. A seasonal cycle would see the lake fill at about the same time every year.

questions.stem: A monitoring record of a river shows high flows every winter and low flows every summer, with a very large flood in only two of 40 years. How should a planner use this record?
options: Treat seasonal flows as predictable and plan for rare floods as a risk
Treat the two large floods as a cycle that will recur every 20 years
Treat all flow changes as unpredictable, so no planning is possible
Treat the seasonal pattern as unreliable because floods interrupt it
questions.explanation: The winter-summer pattern is a reliable cycle, while the big floods are irregular events best handled as risks with an estimated probability. Two floods in 40 years do not show a regular 20-year cycle.

questions.stem: Cliffs near Port Willunga show layers of marine limestone containing shell fossils, now well above sea level. What past change in sphere interactions does this suggest?
options: The area was once a desert, and the limestone formed from wind-blown dust
The area was once covered by ice, and the shells were dropped by glaciers
The area was once under the sea and has since been raised or the sea has fallen
The area has always been above the sea, and the shells were carried by birds
questions.explanation: Marine limestone with shell fossils forms on the sea floor, so its presence above sea level means sea level has fallen relative to the land or the land has been uplifted. This is an example of reading past interactions from the rock record.

questions.stem: A sediment core from a lake shows a layer rich in charcoal, then a layer of coarse sand, then a return to fine mud with abundant pollen. Which past sequence of events is most likely?
options: A volcanic eruption deposited sand, which later burnt to form charcoal
A fire removed vegetation, erosion washed in sand, then plants recovered
A flood deposited charcoal, plants then died, and later wind brought in sand
A drought killed fish, the lake then froze, and plants then disappeared
questions.explanation: Charcoal records fire; bare ground after a fire erodes easily, sending coarse sediment into the lake; renewed pollen shows vegetation returned. Reading the layers from bottom to top gives the order of events.

questions.stem: A council wants to predict how a low-lying coastal suburb will change over the next 50 years. Which combination of data would give the best basis for a prediction?
options: Past shoreline positions, sea-level trends and storm records for the area
Present house prices, population numbers and traffic counts in the area
Today's tide time, wind speed and air temperature at the local beach
The rock types of the area and the age of the oldest fossils found in its cliffs
questions.explanation: Predictions of coastal change rest on how the shoreline has changed, how sea level is trending and how often damaging storms occur. Single-day weather readings and fossil ages say little about the next 50 years.

questions.stem: A model predicts a wetland will dry out by 2060 if current groundwater pumping continues. Why should this prediction be presented with its uncertainty?
options: Groundwater pumping has no effect on wetland water levels in most settings
Future rainfall, pumping rates and land use may differ from the assumptions
Models of Earth systems are guesses that are not based on any measurements
Wetlands cannot change within only a few decades, so the model must be wrong
questions.explanation: A prediction depends on its assumptions, and future rainfall, pumping and land use are uncertain, so the outcome is a range rather than a certainty. Models are built from measurements, and wetlands can change quickly when water tables fall.

questions.stem: In the field, a geologist records the strike and dip of a tilted bed of sandstone. What does the dip describe?
options: The compass direction of a horizontal line on the bed
The thickness of the bed measured at right angles
The height of the bed above the local sea level
The angle the bed slopes down from the horizontal
questions.explanation: Dip is the angle of steepest slope of the bed below the horizontal, measured at right angles to the strike. Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on the bedding surface.

questions.stem: Before field work at a local creek, students study satellite images of the catchment. What is the main value of this secondary data?
options: It replaces the need to collect any primary data at the creek itself
It measures the dissolved oxygen in the creek water from above
It proves which human activity is causing any change in the creek
It shows land use and features across the whole catchment, beyond the site
questions.explanation: Satellite images give a catchment-wide view of vegetation, farms and urban areas that helps explain what is measured at the site. They cannot measure water chemistry directly or prove a cause on their own.

questions.stem: After a crude oil spill, some oil evaporates, some coats seabirds and some soaks into beach gravel, where it persists for years. Which statement about sphere interactions is correct?
options: One event in the biosphere affects the atmosphere but no other sphere
One event in the atmosphere affects the geosphere but no other sphere
One event in the hydrosphere affects the atmosphere, biosphere and geosphere
One event in the geosphere affects the hydrosphere but no other sphere
questions.explanation: Oil spilled at sea partly evaporates into the air, harms wildlife and is trapped in shoreline sediment, so a single event in the water spreads to all the other spheres. Oil in gravel can persist long after the surface has been cleaned.

questions.stem: The planetary boundaries framework identifies limits for Earth-system processes such as climate change, biodiversity loss and nitrogen and phosphorus flows. What idea about the Earth system does it rest on?
options: Human pressure on one process can push the whole Earth system past safe limits
Each Earth-system process is independent, so it can be managed on its own
The Earth system always returns to its earlier state, whatever the pressure
Only the atmosphere matters, because the other spheres cannot be changed
questions.explanation: The framework treats the processes as interlinked parts of one system, so crossing one boundary raises the risk of changes in the others. Its aim is to define a safe operating space for human activity.
